base_properties.human_readable: Tenure Peer Review as Demographic Gatekeeping

commentary.narrative_context: Tenure peer review is nominally a meritocratic system in which experienced researchers evaluate candidates' scholarly contributions and ability to work within a discipline. This constraint reading frames tenure peer review as a mechanism for demographic gatekeeping: the 'fit' and 'collegiality' criteria deployed during peer review operate as cover stories for selective reproduction of dominant demographic groups. The reading does not claim that individual evaluators consciously discriminate; rather, that evaluation standards are interpreted through the unexamined norms of majority-group scholarship, communication, and professional networks. Candidates from underrepresented demographics face higher evidentiary burdens on research productivity while facing rejection on cultural grounds that are rarely made explicit or contestable. The measurement series spans 1970–2026, capturing both the post-civil rights integration of academia and the contemporary crisis of contingent labor.
commentary.kernel_context: This constraint is one reading of the contested tenure_contract kernel. The reading instantiates: demographic_reproduction_reading. The sibling readings are: academic_freedom_reading (tenure decouples researcher survival from institutional backlash, enabling high-risk inquiry) and institutional_extraction_reading (tenure enables permanent rent extraction by early winners, loading costs onto contingent labor). The demographic_reproduction_reading frames tenure peer review as demographic closure: the same peer-review apparatus that can protect inquiry can also protect demographic preservation. The core premise distinguishing this reading from the others is that 'fit' and 'collegiality' criteria, when applied through majority-group norms, systematically exclude scholars whose background, methodology, and intellectual traditions diverge from the dominant group. The academic_freedom reading sees peer review as protecting inquiry; this reading sees it as protecting demographic composition. Where academic_freedom emphasizes the research output, demographic_reproduction emphasizes the researcher composition. These readings coexist as competing interpretations held by different institutional seats (faculty believe the freedom reading; excluded candidates and diversity officers observe the demographic-reproduction reading). The institutional_extraction reading is orthogonal: it addresses the employment-rigidity effects of tenure independent of demographic outcome.
commentary.logic_rationale: Extractiveness is high and rising (0.45→0.71 across the interval). This rising trajectory reflects the strengthening of gatekeeping mechanisms over time: as diversity pressure has increased, the enforcement of 'fit' and 'collegiality' criteria has intensified to maintain demographic composition. Suppression is also high and rising (0.55→0.78), indicating both structural exclusion (institutional barriers) and internalized suppression (candidates internalizing rejection narratives about their 'fit'). Theater ratio is moderate and rising (0.25→0.48), indicating that an increasing share of peer-review activity is devoted to maintaining demographic stability rather than evaluating research. The coercion grid shows class-level suppression and stakes inflation rising most steeply: demographic class experiences the constraint as both higher material stakes (research productivity alone is insufficient to survive evaluation) and higher suppression (gatekeeping operates at the class level, not just individual case-by-case). Resistance at class and organizational levels is non-negligible (0.68 and 0.52 at t_n) but remains structurally constrained: candidates at the powerless individual level cannot organize resistance within the institutions that evaluate them.
commentary.perspectival_gap: Majority-group faculty compute the constraint as rope or even mountain (natural meritocratic evaluation): from their position, 'fit' and 'collegiality' are obvious criteria for assessing scholarly quality and departmental functionality. Underrepresented candidates compute it as snare: 'fit' operates as a rejection criterion applied asymmetrically, and 'collegiality' is interpreted through majority-group norms they cannot conform to without abandoning their own intellectual traditions. The directive-chain effect: department hiring committees (institutional power, demographic majority, arbitrage exit) experience the constraint as meritocratic self-defense; underrepresented candidates (powerless, identity-locked exit) experience it as structural closure. Institutional administration observes both framings simultaneously but lacks enforcement mechanisms to alter evaluation standards without triggering academic freedom defense.
commentary.directionality_logic: Majority-group faculty benefit from the constraint without bearing its costs; directionality approaches the beneficiary end (d ≈ 0.2–0.3). Underrepresented candidates bear the extraction cost (higher burden of proof, implicit rejection criteria, constrained exit to contingent positions) without benefiting from it; directionality approaches the target end (d ≈ 0.8–0.9). The suppression mechanism is partly structural (institutional barriers, legal constraints on hiring remedies) and partly internalized (candidates internalize 'not a fit' narratives, fuse identity with academic work while facing systematic rejection, remain in contingent positions that lack upward mobility). Contingent faculty occupy a dual position: they bear extraction (teaching loads, research with no tenure security) and are systematically excluded from the evaluation process itself (their voices are absent from hiring committees). Exit for both victim groups is severely constrained by professional identity fusion: candidates have spent years preparing for academic careers, have skills not easily transferable to other sectors, and face a labor market that devalues career interruption.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The classification prevents misreading the constraint as a rope or mountain. A rope reading would miss that peer review operates with asymmetric beneficiary/victim structure and active suppression of exit (rival hiring systems, alternative career paths). A mountain reading would falsely treat demographic closure as a natural outcome of meritocratic evaluation. The snare classification captures the core structure: tenure peer review persists because it benefits the majority-group beneficiaries (secure jobs, control of evaluation standards, demographic preservation) who have both power and exit options (can retire, can publish outside, can change institutions), while it extracts from the powerless victims (underrepresented candidates with identity-locked exit, contingent faculty with trapped exit) who cannot reorganize the system. The vindicated proposition (academic_freedom_doctrine) masks the mechanism: the defense of peer review as essential to academic freedom prevents scrutiny of how peer review operates as demographic closure. This is the false-summit signature: a doctrine that appears to protect inquiry in fact protects demographic composition.

omegas.question: Are 'fit' and 'collegiality' criteria applied according to implicit, demographically-inflected norms, or according to explicit, research-productivity-based metrics that can be documented and audited?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Mandate transparent documentation of evaluation criteria and decision rationales on every tenure case (as some legal jurisdictions now require); audit whether criteria are applied identically across demographic groups; track whether research productivity is the actual decision driver or whether implicit cultural criteria overrule productivity differences.
omegas.impact: If criteria are genuinely implicit and demographic-inflected, the constraint's extractiveness rises (from 0.71 to 0.80+) and snare classification is reinforced. If criteria are documented and applied consistently, extractiveness drops toward rope classification (0.40–0.50 range) and the demographic closure mechanism is disrupted.
omegas.description: Whether peer-review criteria are applied as explicit research metrics or implicit demographic-alignment filters.

omegas.question: What portion of the measured suppression (0.78) is attributable to structural exclusion (institutional barriers, legal constraints, lack of alternative pathways) versus internalized suppression (candidates silencing their own intellectual traditions, internalizing rejection narratives)?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Post-exit interview studies: track whether scholars who leave academia experience suppression persistence after external barriers are removed; measure whether self-silencing and identity-fusion persist even when structural constraints are lifted. Contrast exit trajectories for contingent faculty (identity-locked) versus candidates who leave before tenure application (constrained exit).
omegas.impact: If suppression is primarily structural, external policy intervention (transparency mandates, alternative hiring systems, legal enforcement) can disrupt the constraint. If suppression is primarily internalized, the constraint persists even after structural barriers are removed — the reproduction mechanism has been absorbed into candidates' self-perception. A finding of substantial internalized suppression would classify this as a deeper snare than structural suppression alone, with higher theatre_ratio (the performance is internalized; candidates police their own gatekeeping).
omegas.description: Mechanism underlying the measured suppression: structural barriers or internalized identity fusion.

omegas.question: Within a single academic institution, can both the academic_freedom_reading and the demographic_reproduction_reading coexist as empirically valid framings of the same peer-review process, or does adopting one reading logically preclude the other?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Institutional case studies: document whether the same peer-review process that protects (or fails to protect) academic inquiry simultaneously operates as demographic gatekeeping. Can a single peer-review rubric satisfy both readings, or are they structurally incompatible within one institution's evaluation system?
omegas.impact: If the readings coexist (both are empirically true of the same system), the constraint's classification depends on which stakeholder seat is being evaluated (majority-group faculty see academic freedom protection; underrepresented candidates see demographic gatekeeping). If the readings are incompatible, one reading is mischaracterizing the system — either peer review is protecting inquiry and not gatekeeping (academic_freedom_reading forecloses demographic_reproduction), or peer review is gatekeeping and the 'inquiry protection' claim is cover story (demographic_reproduction_reading forecloses academic_freedom). The engine's per-seat classification will flag this divergence; the omega documents whether the divergence is real structure or evaluator mischaracterization.
omegas.description: Whether the academic_freedom and demographic_reproduction readings are empirically coexistent or logically incompatible interpretations of the same peer-review system.

omegas.question: Are contingent faculty who perform research and mentoring within a department rendered structurally invisible in tenure peer-review processes (excluded from teaching load calculations, from graduate student mentoring credit, from research collaboration recognition)?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Departmental audit of tenure-evaluation rubrics: document whether contingent faculty contributions are listed, weighted, or accounted for in any form in tenure decisions. Interview tenure committees about whether contingent faculty productivity affects tenure candidates' demonstrated teaching or mentoring capacity.
omegas.impact: If contingent faculty labor is rendered invisible, the cost extraction increases (contingent faculty bear costs; majority-group tenure-track faculty benefit from their labor being absorbed into department resources). The theatre_ratio rises (tenured faculty can appear to be doing all the teaching/mentoring when contingent faculty actually perform most of it). The constraint's classification strengthens toward snare (systematic invisibility is a suppression mechanism that prevents contingent faculty from claiming their contributions or organizing around their exclusion).
omegas.description: Whether contingent faculty labor is systematically rendered invisible in tenure-evaluation systems.

network.dual_formulation_note: This constraint is one reading of the contested tenure_contract kernel. The demographic_reproduction_reading frames tenure peer review as reproducing dominant group composition through implicit 'fit' criteria. The academic_freedom_reading frames tenure as decoupling researcher survival from institutional backlash. The institutional_extraction_reading frames tenure as enabling employment rigidity and cost-loading onto contingent labor. All three readings address the same institutional apparatus (peer-review tenure decisions) but instantiate different constraints with different beneficiary/victim structures and ε values. They coexist as competing interpretations held by different institutional seats. Each constraint story is ε-invariant: the ε for demographic reproduction (0.71) addresses the extraction of access/stability from underrepresented candidates; the ε for academic freedom would address the degree of researcher protection (likely lower, 0.2–0.3); the ε for institutional extraction would address employment rigidity costs (likely 0.60–0.70). The kernel contest is whether peer review's primary function is (a) protecting inquiry, (b) reproducing demographics, or (c) extracting rents — structurally distinct claims about the same apparatus.
